d: Generation seven married an Annecchino — Now the largest surname in this archive, ahead of Falco itself — and on 10 September 2026 it gave up the name of Filomena's mother.
Everywhere this family has been recorded — Six towns of the Valle Caudina, one cemetery in Brisbane — and, underneath, the nineteen streets of one small town that carry almost all of the evidence.

${changes.length} changes, ${byDay.length} working days — Generated from this archive's own commit history, not written by hand — so it cannot drift from what actually happened. Every entry is a real commit and links to it.

${rows.length} things this archive got wrong and says so — Every correction is kept on the page it corrects. Nothing here has been deleted — the wrong reading stays beside the right one, because the failure is usually the more useful half.
The family the Falco married eleven times — Generations one and three both married a Crisci. So did five Falco daughters, in the other direction — and the last of them married one in Australia.

Nine generations, the ninth living and named — From the Arienzo of the 1730s to Brisbane. Each generation is joined to the one above it by a record that names a father — except the first, where the line stops.

Two tests, generation eight — Carmine Falco and Francesca Zampiello were tested. The result is not a surprise — it is a confirmation — and the two most useful things on this page are what the test refuses to claim and how far back it can see.

Eleven families, not one surname — A family history that follows only one surname is half a history. These are the families the Falco married — what is known of each in its own right, how often they married in, and where the evidence for them stops.
The Zampiello maternal name — Giuseppa Ferrara married Angelo Zampiello and became Francesca's mother — and until now the Zampiello page did not name her once.
${rows.length} plates, every one of them evidence — Every image this archive holds, in one contact sheet, oldest first. Click any of them for the transcription and the citation.

${rows.length} burials at Nudgee, Brisbane — Where the line ends up. Every burial this archive has found in Australia, with its plot — and what the plots do and do not prove about who lies beside whom.

Several Falco, one town — Falco is a name that was coined independently, many times, in many places — so there is no single Falco family to find. What there is, at Arienzo, is a handful of separate Falco strands living in the same parish and often the same street. This is what each of them is, and w
Generation six married a Maione — Costanza Maione of Arienzo — the mother of Carminantonio, and the one wife in the spine whose own birth record has actually been found.

${couples.length} couples the archive can name — Who married whom, where the archive knows it — and, on every row, whether it knows because a clerk wrote it down, because the line argues it, or because the family tree says so.

The families who joined this one — ${other.length} surnames married into the Falco line. ${named} of their people are named here; ${withheld} more are alive and are not published. If one of these is your family, this page is for you.

The house the line married into — ${all.length} Morgillo are recorded in this archive. Until 2026 almost none of them were joined to each other. The Arienzo death registers of 1826, 1827 and 1828, read act by act, put two Morgillo households on the ground for the first time.

Every record this archive has found — ${register.length} entries for ${distinct} distinct names, ${linked} of them with a link to the source that names them; the other ${unlinked} say in the Source column why no link exists. This is the raw catch — not a family tree, and most of it is not this famil

Generation two married a Rivetti — Chiara Rivetti, who outlived Pasquale Falco by nine years — and the two Rivetti families of Arienzo, one of them gentry, that the archive spent five years telling apart.

Three hundred years, six regimes, one parish — Arienzo did not sit still under one flag while this family was in it. Spanish viceroys, Austrians, Bourbons, the French, the Bourbons again, then Italy — and four kilometres away, across a border, a papal enclave. The bands are who governed the place; t

Coverage, including the years that held nothing — Twenty-one annual registers read page by page — ${totalImgs} images, some two thousand acts, ${totalFalco} Falco. This page exists so that a null is not lost: knowing a volume has been read and held nothing is worth as much as knowing what it held.

Nine generations, three hundred years, and what has actually been read — The line, the regimes it lived under, and — laid underneath — the exact years of register this archive has read act by act. The gaps in that band are the honest part.
Nine generations, drawn — The whole documented line in one figure — each generation, who they married, which child carried the line, and every sibling the archive can name beside them.
